rationale: A wins because it knows where the evidence ends and makes proof the point: "whether 'pilot' means a funded production trial, a security review, or a sandbox" is exactly the question a real reporter will ask. B has useful shapes, especially "Notion ships offline editing, the feature cloud-native software spent a decade treating as optional," but it overstates the record with "What it took for a 100M-user productivity app to clear a bank's security review" when the update only says pilots. That is the difference between press strategy and making a reporter fact-check you before they read sentence two.
gaps_in_A: "Notion ships offline mode" is refused too quickly. At ~100M users, offline editing with sync on reconnect could be a real product/infrastructure engineering angle if Notion can produce conflict-resolution and scope detail.
"consumer-grade scale = banned shadow IT" is a plausible contrarian lens, but it is not in the update. A flags the proof gap, but the angle still leans on an unproven industry assumption.
The set stays heavily inside regulated-enterprise/security. That is defensible, but it leaves the offline-first launch underused as its own technical story.
gaps_in_B: "What it took for a 100M-user productivity app to clear a bank's security review" invents clearance. The facts say four banks run pilots, not that Notion cleared security review.
"what software the biggest US banks actually approve and deploy" overclaims twice. A pilot is not deployment, and approval may only mean permission to test.
"cloud-native software spent a decade treating as optional" is a big industry thesis with no supplied support. It can be a reported question; stated as fact, it is decoration.
The next step, "journalist-fit-check," is premature. Before matching reporters, this needs source confirmation or news-search around the bank pilots and security claims.
